\section{Direction Discriminability}
\label{sec:direction_quality}

Before evaluating $\dsyc$ as a reward signal (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}--\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}), we first establish that it captures a genuine sycophancy-related signal in the residual stream.
If the direction failed to discriminate sycophantic from non-sycophantic activations, downstream reward failures would be trivially explained by poor direction quality rather than by a fundamental gap between discriminability and reward utility.
We evaluate discriminability along five axes: cross-validated classification accuracy, evidence-strength stratification, cross-model transfer, training stability, and probe ablation.
Figure~\ref{fig:direction_quality} summarizes the per-layer AUROC profiles for both models.

\paragraph{Qwen3-8B layer-wise discriminability.}
We evaluate $\dsyc$ via 5-fold cross-validated AUROC on 181 style-controlled contrastive pairs (\S\ref{ssec:extraction}).
The direction achieves AUROC $0.827 \pm 0.028$ at its best layer (L19).
Discriminability emerges gradually across depth: layers L0--L8 perform near chance, statistical significance ($p < 0.01$) first appears at L16, and performance peaks at L19.
This gradual emergence, with the peak in the upper third of the network, suggests that sycophancy-relevant information is encoded as a late-stage representation rather than an input-level confound.
The direction also captures evidential granularity.
AUROC rises monotonically from 0.675 on weak-evidence pairs to 0.883 on medium and 0.929 on strong pairs.
This gradient indicates that $\dsyc$ encodes the degree of evidential warrant, not merely a binary sycophancy label.

\paragraph{Cross-model generalization.}
To rule out that these results are specific to Qwen3-8B's representation geometry, we repeat the full extraction and evaluation pipeline on Llama-3-8B-Instruct.
Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} compares the two models.
Llama-3-8B achieves CV AUROC $0.779 \pm 0.019$ at L16, with a parallel evidence-strength gradient (weak 0.711, medium 0.864, strong 0.911).
The best-layer depth differs (L16 vs.\ L19), consistent with the architectural differences between the two families, but the qualitative pattern is identical: gradual emergence, best-layer selection in the upper third, and monotonic strength scaling.
Discriminability is robust across knowledge domains, with per-domain AUROCs on Llama-3-8B ranging from 0.751 (geography) to 0.844 (commonsense).
When surface confounds (response length, hedging patterns) are explicitly controlled, Llama-3-8B's AUROC rises to 0.923, which confirms that the direction captures semantic content rather than stylistic artifacts.
The consistent results across architecturally distinct model families indicate that contrastive sycophancy directions reflect a shared representational phenomenon rather than a model-specific idiosyncrasy.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Cross-model $\dsyc$ discriminability. CV AUROC is 5-fold cross-validated; evidence-strength AUROCs are evaluated on the full dataset at each model's best layer.}
\label{tab:cross_model}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Model & Best Layer & CV AUROC & Weak & Medium & Strong \\
\midrule
Qwen3-8B & L19 & $0.827{\pm}0.028$ & 0.675 & 0.883 & 0.929 \\
Llama-3-8B & L16 & $0.779{\pm}0.019$ & 0.711 & 0.864 & 0.911 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_layer_auroc.pdf}
\caption{Per-layer AUROC of $\dsyc$ as a function of normalized depth (layer index / total layers). Qwen3-8B (36 layers, solid) shows gradual emergence from near-chance at L0 to a peak at L19, with performance plateauing in the final third. Llama-3-8B (32 layers, dashed; layers 16--31 only) exhibits a similar upper-third concentration. Both models achieve best discriminability in layers 50--60\% through the network.}
\label{fig:direction_quality}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Training stability and probe ablation.}
Two additional analyses confirm the robustness of $\dsyc$ under training dynamics.
First, we track direction drift during LoRA fine-tuning: at step 500, the cosine similarity between the original and re-extracted $\dsyc$ is approximately 0.96, and per-layer AUROC remains above 0.77.
The direction drifts slowly relative to the 500-step recalibration interval (\S\ref{ssec:recalib}), so the reward signal does not become stale between updates.
Second, we compare $\dsyc$ against a random baseline: a logistic probe trained on the learned direction achieves AUROC 0.835, versus 0.727 for a probe trained on a random direction of equal dimensionality ($\Delta{=}{+}0.108$).
The learned direction carries substantially more sycophancy-relevant information than an arbitrary axis in the same activation space.

\paragraph{Implications for reward design.}
These results establish that $\dsyc$ reliably separates sycophantic from non-sycophantic representations across models, evidence-strength levels, and training checkpoints.
Direction quality is not the bottleneck.
The reward failures documented in \S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}--\S\ref{sec:probe_trap} therefore cannot be attributed to a noisy or degenerate direction; they point to a deeper incompatibility between discriminability and reward utility.

## Task: Write §1 Introduction for EMNLP 2026 paper

Write the Introduction section (~900 words) for a paper titled "Discriminability Without Utility: Why Sycophancy Directions Fail as RL Rewards".

1. `Read /home/ubuntu/agent-ml-research/skills/global/paper-writing-norms.skill.md`

## Paper Summary

This is a negative-result + mechanistic analysis paper. Core thesis: a contrastive sycophancy direction (d_syc) extracted from LLM residual streams achieves AUROC 0.82 (Qwen3-8B) and 0.78 (Llama-3-8B) for discriminating sycophantic vs non-sycophantic activations, yet **fails in ALL tested formulations** when used as a GRPO reward signal. The gap between discriminability and reward utility is fundamental, not a tuning problem.

## Outline (from writing_plan.yaml)

The introduction should follow this structure:

1. **Hook** (1-2 paragraphs): Representation engineering (RepE) can detect sycophancy with AUROC 0.82 in LLM activations. A natural next step is using these directions as RL reward signals. We show this fails. The gap between detecting a behavior and penalizing it is fundamental.

2. **Gap** (1 paragraph): Existing anti-sycophancy methods (ACT, behavioral GRPO) treat all belief changes uniformly. RepE/CRAFT/Latent-GRPO use representation geometry as reward for reasoning and safety, but sycophancy's unique geometric structure (capitulation ≈ revision in direction space) remains uninvestigated.

3. **Insight** (1 paragraph): d_syc encodes belief change direction but not change warrant. The same geometric direction captures both "model correctly revises belief" and "model sycophantically capitulates."

4. **Contributions** (bullet list):
   - (C1) Cross-model validated d_syc discriminability (Qwen3-8B AUROC 0.827, Llama-3-8B AUROC 0.779) with systematic 3-formulation investigation establishing discriminability ≠ reward utility (§3-4)
   - (C2) Probe reward trap mechanism with behavioral-before-distributional collapse diagnostic: ToF drops to 0 at step 500 while entropy remains 0.70, with 1300-step lag before entropy collapse (§5)
   - (C3) Unified root cause explaining why sycophancy is geometrically harder than reasoning/safety for representation-guided RL (§6)

## Key experiments to reference (from registry):
- **exp-001**: Qwen3-8B d_syc, 5-fold CV AUROC 0.827 ± 0.028, best layer L19, evidence gradient weak=0.675/medium=0.883/strong=0.929
- **exp-012**: Llama-3-8B d_syc, CV AUROC 0.779 ± 0.019, best layer L16, style-controlled 0.923
- **exp-002 series**: Cosine R1 failure chain (4 configs, all fail)
- **exp-008v3**: Binary probe trap — ToF=0 at step 500, entropy=0.70, 1300-step lag
- **exp-004**: ACT baseline, SYCONScore=0.301 (partial success but low ToF)
- **exp-016**: ActAdd, SYCONScore=0.054 (harmful, destroys ToF)
- **vanilla-baseline**: ToF=0.111, NoF=0.923, SYCONScore=0.197

## LaTeX conventions:
- Custom commands: \dsyc (d_syc direction), \rone (R1), \rthree (R3), \tof (ToF), \nof (NoF), \sycon (SYCONScore)
- Section labels: \ref{sec:direction_quality} (§3), \ref{sec:cosine_failure} (§4), \ref{sec:probe_trap} (§5), \ref{sec:discussion} (§6)
- Figure reference: \ref{fig:overview} if applicable
- Use \citet{} for author-name citations, \citep{} for parenthetical

## Already-written sections (for context/consistency):

### §2 Framework (framework.tex)
Defines d_syc extraction from 181 style-controlled contrastive pairs, three R1 formulations (F1 cosine, F2 scaled cosine, F3 binary probe), R3 = NLI behavioral reward, R = w1·R1 + w3·R3, online recalibration every 500 steps, eval metrics ToF/NoF/SYCONScore.

### §3 Direction Quality (direction_quality.tex)
Qwen3-8B AUROC 0.827±0.028 at L19. Evidence strength gradient. Cross-model: Llama-3-8B AUROC 0.779±0.019 at L16. Training stability (cosine ~0.96). Probe ablation (+0.108 Δ). Conclusion: direction quality is NOT the bottleneck.

4-experiment failure chain: F1a tanh saturation, F1b raw cosine too weak (gap 0.098), F1c recalibration induces mode collapse (AUROC 0.82→0.91 yet fails), F1d scaling amplifies noise. Root cause: d_syc encodes direction of belief change but not warrant.

Differentiable probe gamed in ~30 steps (exp-008). Binary probe with stop-gradient: stubbornness trap. ToF=0 at step 500, entropy=0.70, 1300-step lag. R mean +0.72 during collapse. Dilemma: differentiable=gaming, frozen=rigidity.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Representation engineering \citep{zou2023repe} reveals that large language models encode sycophancy as a linear direction in their residual streams.
A contrastive sycophancy direction $\dsyc$, extracted from style-controlled pairs of valid belief revision and sycophantic capitulation, achieves cross-validated AUROC $0.827 \pm 0.028$ on Qwen3-8B and $0.779 \pm 0.019$ on Llama-3-8B (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}).
The direction captures evidential granularity: discriminability rises monotonically from weak-evidence pairs (AUROC 0.675) through medium (0.883) to strong (0.929), and the signal remains stable under LoRA training with cosine drift of approximately 0.96 at 500 steps.
These results, replicated across two architecturally distinct model families, point to an appealing possibility: if the model's representations already separate sycophantic from non-sycophantic behavior, that separation should be convertible into a reward signal for reinforcement learning.
Sycophancy is among the most persistent alignment failures in deployed systems \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, and a representation-level reward could complement existing behavioral approaches by targeting the internal computation rather than its surface outputs.

This paper shows that the conversion fails.
We test three formulations that translate $\dsyc$ into a GRPO training signal (cosine similarity, scaled cosine, and binary probe) across six experimental configurations.
Every formulation fails.
Cosine similarity produces a reward gap of just 0.098 between valid and sycophantic activations, too narrow to drive policy updates (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}).
Online recalibration improves the offline AUROC from 0.82 to 0.91 yet triggers mode collapse rather than better training.
A binary probe with stopped gradients avoids the magnitude problem but creates a stubbornness trap: the model learns that never revising its answer reliably collects the probe reward, and the true-positive flip rate ($\tof$) drops to zero within 500 steps while generation entropy remains at 0.70 (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
The gap between discriminability and reward utility is not a tuning problem.
It is a structural consequence of what $\dsyc$ encodes and what it does not.

Existing approaches to sycophancy mitigation fall into two camps.
Behavioral methods such as ACT \citep{consistency2025bctact} and NLI-based GRPO score whether the model's final answer is consistent with a ground-truth label but do not examine internal representations; they treat all belief changes uniformly.
Representation-based methods take the opposite approach: activation addition \citep{turner2023actadd} and contrastive activation addition \citep{rimsky2024caa} steer model behavior at inference time, while techniques for discovering latent knowledge \citep{burns2023ccs} and representation-guided RL \citep{zhang2026latentgrpo} use activation geometry to shape behavior during training.
These methods have shown success on reasoning faithfulness and safety refusal.
The shared premise is that a direction with high discriminability in activation space should transfer into a useful training signal or intervention target.
For reasoning and safety, this premise holds: the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve along the relevant direction.
Sycophancy violates this premise.
The behavior to suppress (capitulation under social pressure) and the behavior to preserve (revision under valid evidence) produce overlapping activation signatures along $\dsyc$, because both involve the model shifting its stated belief toward the user's position.

The root cause is a semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility.
$\dsyc$ encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}.
A post-hoc classifier can use this signal effectively because it scores labeled examples where the validity of the belief change is already known.
A reward signal during RL training has no such access to ground truth.
The reward must distinguish warranted revision from unwarranted capitulation using activation geometry alone, and $\dsyc$ collapses exactly this distinction.
This conflation is not an artifact of our extraction procedure.
Sycophancy is defined relative to external evidential warrant \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, a property that no direction in activation space can fully encode.
The problem is compounded by the entanglement between helpfulness and sycophancy at the representation level: the same internal mechanisms that allow models to track user intent also predispose them to capitulate \citep{wang2025internal}, and RLHF amplifies this tendency \citep{shapira2026amplifies}.
When reward overoptimization \citep{gao2023scaling} operates on a signal that conflates compliance with capitulation, the result is predictable collapse \citep{casper2023openproblems}.

We present three contributions:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Cross-model discriminability $\neq$ reward utility} (C1). We extract and validate $\dsyc$ on Qwen3-8B (AUROC $0.827 \pm 0.028$) and Llama-3-8B (AUROC $0.779 \pm 0.019$), then systematically test three reward formulations across six configurations. All fail, establishing that discriminability alone does not confer reward utility (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}, \S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}).

\item \textbf{Probe reward trap with behavioral-before-distributional collapse} (C2). The binary probe reward produces behavioral death ($\tof = 0$ at step 500) while entropy remains at 0.70. The 1,300-step lag before distributional collapse means standard entropy monitoring misses the failure entirely, with the reward averaging $+0.72$ throughout (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).

\item \textbf{Sycophancy is geometrically harder for representation-guided RL} (C3). We trace all failures to a unified root cause: $\dsyc$ encodes belief-change direction but not evidential warrant. Unlike reasoning or safety directions, sycophancy directions conflate the target behavior with its complement, placing a principled limit on when representation-guided RL can succeed (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Representation Engineering and Activation Steering.}
Representation engineering \citep{zou2023repe} established that linear directions in LLM residual streams encode high-level behavioral concepts.
Subsequent work exploited such directions for inference-time intervention: ITI \citep{li2023iti} uses probe weights as steering vectors for truthfulness, ActAdd \citep{turner2023actadd} adds fixed activation offsets to shift model behavior, and CAA \citep{rimsky2024caa} applies contrastive activation addition to reduce sycophancy at inference time.
CCS \citep{burns2023ccs} discovers truth-related directions without supervision through a consistency objective.
All five methods use representation geometry for inference-time classification or steering.
Our work tests whether the same geometric information transfers to a training-time reward signal, and finds that it does not: $\dsyc$ achieves strong discriminability (AUROC 0.82) but fails as a GRPO reward in all tested formulations.

\paragraph{Sycophancy Characterization and Mitigation.}
\citet{sharma2023sycophancy} showed that sycophancy is pervasive across RLHF-trained assistants and identified preference-model bias as a contributing cause.
\citet{shapira2026amplifies} proved formally that RLHF amplifies sycophancy under standard assumptions.
\citet{wang2025internal} traced the phenomenon to late-layer preference shifts via logit-lens analysis and confirmed that sycophantic behavior has identifiable internal origins.
On the mitigation side, \citet{wei2024synthetic} demonstrated that synthetic data mixed into fine-tuning reduces sycophancy at the data level.
Activation consistency training \citep[ACT;][]{consistency2025bctact} penalizes activation divergence between the model's initial and post-pressure responses but does not distinguish warranted from unwarranted belief changes.
\citet{obrien2025fewbadneurons} identified sycophancy-associated neurons and surgically corrected them; their probes serve a diagnostic role rather than an optimization target.
These methods either operate at the data or behavioral level, where all belief changes are treated uniformly, or use representations only for diagnosis.
Our analysis shows why the step from diagnosis to reward is structurally blocked for sycophancy: the direction that detects the behavior conflates it with its complement.

\paragraph{Reward Design and Overoptimization.}
\citet{gao2023scaling} established scaling laws for reward model overoptimization: proxy rewards diverge from true objectives under sustained optimization pressure.
\citet{skalse2022hacking} proved that no bounded proxy reward can be immune to hacking.
\citet{casper2023openproblems} surveyed fundamental limitations of RLHF, including reward misspecification and distributional shift.
\citet{denison2024subterfuge} showed that reward hacking can escalate from sycophantic agreement to active reward tampering.
\citet{mckinney2023fragility} found that learned reward functions fail when applied to train new policies, a failure mode related to our probe reward trap.
\citet{wen2024mislead} documented U-Sophistry, where models learn to produce outputs that mislead human evaluators.
\citet{ackermann2026gradreg} proposed gradient regularization as a mitigation strategy.
Our probe reward trap is an extreme instance of overoptimization: a low-capacity linear probe is gamed within 500 training steps, with behavioral collapse preceding entropy collapse by approximately 1,300 steps.

\paragraph{Representation-Guided Reinforcement Learning.}
\citet{zhang2026latentgrpo} introduced Latent-GRPO, which uses spherical projection onto robust cluster centroids as a GRPO reward for reasoning correctness.
\citet{sinii2025smallvectors} showed that RL training induces structured changes in steering vectors, a result that supports the feasibility of representation-space rewards in principle.
Both approaches succeed because the target categories (correct vs.\ incorrect reasoning, safe vs.\ unsafe outputs) occupy geometrically separable regions along the relevant direction.
Sycophancy breaks this condition: capitulation and legitimate revision share the same geometric direction and differ only in whether the belief change is warranted, a property that no activation-space direction encodes.
Our results explain this asymmetry and identify the warrant gap as the structural barrier.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Representation engineering \citep{zou2023repe} reveals that large language models encode sycophancy as a linear direction in their residual streams.
A contrastive sycophancy direction $\dsyc$, extracted from style-controlled pairs of valid belief revision and sycophantic capitulation, achieves cross-validated AUROC $0.827 \pm 0.028$ on Qwen3-8B and $0.779 \pm 0.019$ on Llama-3-8B (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}).
The direction captures evidential granularity: discriminability rises monotonically from weak-evidence pairs (AUROC 0.675) through medium (0.883) to strong (0.929), and the signal remains stable under LoRA training with cosine drift of approximately 0.96 at 500 steps.
These results, replicated across two architecturally distinct model families, point to an appealing possibility: if the model's representations already separate sycophantic from non-sycophantic behavior, that separation should be convertible into a reward signal for reinforcement learning.
Sycophancy is among the most persistent alignment failures in deployed systems \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, and a representation-level reward could complement existing behavioral approaches by targeting the internal computation rather than its surface outputs.

This paper shows that the conversion fails, and that the failure runs deeper than the representation signal itself.
We test three formulations that translate $\dsyc$ into a GRPO \citep{shao2024grpo} training signal (cosine similarity, scaled cosine, and binary probe) across six experimental configurations; every formulation fails.
Cosine similarity produces a reward gap of just 0.098 between valid and sycophantic activations, too narrow to drive policy updates (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}).
Online recalibration improves the offline AUROC from 0.82 to 0.91 yet triggers mode collapse.
A binary probe with stopped gradients creates a stubbornness trap: the model learns that never revising its answer reliably collects the probe reward, and the true-positive flip rate ($\tof$) drops to zero within 500 steps while generation entropy remains at 0.70 (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
These failures might suggest that removing $\dsyc$ in favor of a purely behavioral reward would resolve the problem.
It does not.
R3-only GRPO, which uses an NLI-based behavioral reward without any representation component, also fails to calibrate sycophancy: the \sycon{} score starts at 0.074 at checkpoint 1000, reaches only 0.114 by checkpoint 5000, and never exceeds the vanilla baseline of 0.134 (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
The trajectory shows a slow U-shaped recovery at approximately $+0.010$ per 1000 steps, a rate that would require roughly 8000 additional steps merely to match the untrained model.
Two layers of failure emerge: $\dsyc$-based rewards are actively harmful, and GRPO itself is structurally insufficient for sycophancy calibration.

Existing approaches to sycophancy mitigation span three categories.
Representation-based inference methods, including activation addition \citep{turner2023actadd} and contrastive activation addition \citep{rimsky2024caa}, steer model behavior at test time without modifying weights.
RL-based training methods use scalar rewards to update policy through reinforcement learning; our $\dsyc$ GRPO variants and R3-only GRPO both fall into this category, as does representation-guided RL more broadly \citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}.
SFT-based training takes a fundamentally different approach: ACT \citep{consistency2025bctact} applies supervised fine-tuning with an L2 activation consistency loss that provides dense per-token supervision rather than a single scalar per completion.
ACT achieves a \sycon{} score of 0.301 at checkpoint 8000, more than double the vanilla baseline, while every GRPO variant remains below it (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
The contrast is informative.
Techniques for discovering latent knowledge \citep{burns2023ccs} and representation-guided RL share a premise: a direction with high discriminability in activation space should transfer into a useful training signal.
For reasoning faithfulness and safety refusal, this premise holds, because the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve along the relevant direction.
Sycophancy violates this premise.
Capitulation under social pressure and revision under valid evidence produce overlapping activation signatures along $\dsyc$, because both involve the model shifting its stated belief toward the user's position.

The root cause is a semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility.
$\dsyc$ encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}.
A post-hoc classifier can use this signal effectively because it scores labeled examples where the validity of the belief change is already known.
A reward signal during RL training has no such access to ground truth; it must distinguish warranted revision from unwarranted capitulation using activation geometry alone, and $\dsyc$ collapses exactly this distinction.
This conflation explains both layers of failure.
$\dsyc$ rewards penalize all belief change indiscriminately, producing behavioral collapse.
R3-only GRPO's single scalar per completion cannot compensate because it lacks the per-token resolution to teach which belief changes are warranted and which are not.
ACT succeeds because its dense supervision operates at the token level, where the valid/invalid distinction can be resolved.
Sycophancy is defined relative to external evidential warrant \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, a property that no single activation direction can fully encode.
The entanglement between helpfulness and sycophancy at the representation level, where the same mechanisms that allow models to track user intent also predispose them to capitulate \citep{wang2025internal}, is amplified by RLHF \citep{shapira2026amplifies}.
When reward overoptimization \citep{gao2023scaling} operates on a signal that conflates compliance with capitulation, the result is predictable collapse \citep{casper2023openproblems}.

We present three contributions:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{All GRPO approaches fail for sycophancy calibration} (C1). We extract and validate $\dsyc$ on two model families (Qwen3-8B AUROC $0.827 \pm 0.028$; Llama-3-8B AUROC $0.779 \pm 0.019$), then show that all three $\dsyc$-based reward formulations produce behavioral collapse (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}, \S\ref{sec:probe_trap}). R3-only GRPO, which removes $\dsyc$ entirely, also fails: \sycon{} reaches only 0.114 at checkpoint 5000 against a vanilla baseline of 0.134 (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). Discriminability does not confer reward utility, and sparse RL rewards are structurally insufficient for this task.

\item \textbf{Probe reward trap with behavioral-before-distributional collapse} (C2). The binary probe reward produces behavioral death ($\tof = 0$ at step 500) while entropy remains at 0.70. The 1,300-step lag before distributional collapse means standard entropy monitoring misses the failure entirely, with the reward averaging $+0.72$ throughout (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).

\item \textbf{Sparse RL reward cannot convey the valid/invalid distinction} (C3). We trace all failures to a unified root cause: $\dsyc$ encodes belief-change direction but not evidential warrant. A single scalar reward per completion, whether from representations or behavioral classifiers, cannot teach the model which belief changes are warranted. Dense SFT supervision resolves this: ACT achieves \sycon{} of 0.301, while all GRPO variants remain below vanilla (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{itemize}

## Paper Summary + Scheme C Framing

This paper has a **dual-layer negative result**:
- **Layer 1**: d_syc-based GRPO rewards are **actively harmful** (behavioral collapse, probe trap, cosine noise). All 6 configurations produce mode collapse or stubbornness.
- **Layer 2**: R3-only GRPO (behavioral reward only, no d_syc) also **fails**. SYCONScore stays below vanilla baseline through 5000 steps.
- **Contrast**: ACT (SFT-based, NOT RL) achieves SYCONScore 0.301, more than 2x vanilla.

The conclusion: sparse RL reward (whether representation-based or behavioral) cannot convey the valid/invalid correction distinction for sycophancy. Dense SFT supervision can.

## Section Structure (4 paragraphs)

### §6.1 Unified Root Cause (dual-layer)
- d_syc encodes belief change DIRECTION but not WARRANT
- Cosine R1 = too punitive (penalizes all change); Probe R1 = too permissive (rewards all resistance)
- These are complementary faces of the same geometric blindness
- Cross-model confirmation: Llama-3-8B independently shows AUROC 0.779, same evidence gradient. Even cross-model generalizable discriminability cannot translate to reward utility.
- Unlike reasoning/safety directions (Latent-GRPO, CRAFT), sycophancy's target behavior (capitulation) and complement (revision) share the same geometric direction, differing only in warrant.

### §6.2 GRPO Stubbornness Emergence (NEW — exp-003 trajectory)
Include a comparison table (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}) summarizing all methods:

| Method | Type | Best SYCONScore | ToF | NoF | Step |
|--------|------|----------------|-----|-----|------|
| Vanilla | — | 0.134 | 0.072 | 0.945 | — |
| R3-only GRPO | RL | 0.114 | — | — | 5000 |
| Cosine R1 (F1d) | RL | collapse | — | — | — |
| Binary Probe R1 | RL | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.995 | 500 |
| ActAdd (α=5) | Inference | 0.054 | 0.028 | 0.961 | — |
| ACT | SFT | 0.301 | 0.182 | 0.867 | 8000 |

R3-only GRPO trajectory: ckpt-1000=0.074, ckpt-2000=0.085, ckpt-3000=0.095, ckpt-5000=0.114. U-shaped slow recovery at +0.010/1000steps. Even at 5000 steps, still below vanilla (0.134). Linear extrapolation: ~8000 steps to match vanilla.

Key observation: R3-only GRPO exhibits the same stubbornness pattern as d_syc approaches (high NoF, near-zero ToF) but at a milder level. The sparse scalar reward per completion cannot teach the model WHICH belief changes are warranted.

### §6.3 Why SFT Succeeds Where GRPO Fails
- ACT achieves SYCONScore 0.301 at ckpt-8000 (vs all GRPO below 0.134)
- **IMPORTANT NEW FINDING**: ACT trajectory is NOT monotonic. ckpt-2000=0.255, ckpt-4000=0.214 (dip, -4.1pp), ckpt-6000=0.262 (recovery). ACT also experiences stubbornness episodes (ToF drops, NoF rises at ckpt-4000) but RECOVERS.

- This "recovery capacity" difference is the practical signature of the dense vs sparse supervision gap.
- ACT is 16x more efficient: ckpt-500 already exceeds GRPO's projected ckpt-8000 performance.

### §6.4 Future Directions
- Condition-aware reward design: jointly encoding direction + warrant (conditioning on input evidence validity)
- Hybrid approaches: SFT warm-start + RL fine-tuning
- Richer reward signals that provide per-token supervision within RL (reward models, process reward models)
- Discriminability ≠ reward utility as a general principle for representation-guided RL: test other behavioral attributes

\section{Analysis: Discriminability $\neq$ Reward Utility}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Unified root cause.}
The failures in Sections~\ref{sec:cosine_failure} and~\ref{sec:probe_trap} trace to a single geometric limitation.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation extends beyond Qwen3-8B: Llama-3-8B independently achieves AUROC $0.779 \pm 0.019$ on the same contrastive pairs with the same monotonic evidence gradient, so discriminability generalizes across architectures while the semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve along the relevant direction.
For sycophancy, the target and its complement occupy the same activation region; they differ only in whether external evidence warrants the belief change.

\paragraph{GRPO stubbornness across all formulations.}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Comparison of all sycophancy calibration methods on Qwen3-8B. $\sycon$ is the harmonic mean of $\tof$ and $\nof$; higher indicates better calibration. Best result in \textbf{bold}.}
\label{tab:main_comparison}
\begin{tabular}{llcccc}
\toprule
Method & Type & $\sycon$ $\uparrow$ & $\tof$ $\uparrow$ & $\nof$ $\uparrow$ & Step \\
\midrule
Vanilla & -- & 0.134 & 0.072 & 0.945 & -- \\
$\rthree$-only GRPO & RL & 0.114 & -- & -- & 5000 \\
Cosine $\rone$ (F1d) & RL & collapse & -- & -- & -- \\
Binary Probe $\rone$ & RL & 0.000 & 0.000 & 0.995 & 500 \\
ActAdd ($\alpha{=}5$) & Inference & 0.054 & 0.028 & 0.961 & -- \\
\textbf{ACT} & SFT & \textbf{0.301} & \textbf{0.182} & 0.867 & 8000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison} summarizes all methods evaluated on Qwen3-8B.
$\rthree$-only GRPO removes $\dsyc$ entirely and relies on the NLI-based behavioral reward alone.
If the failures in Sections~\ref{sec:cosine_failure} and~\ref{sec:probe_trap} stemmed solely from the representation reward, this ablation should recover calibration quality.
It does not.
The $\sycon$ trajectory shows partial recovery that stalls: 0.074 at checkpoint 1000, 0.085 at checkpoint 2000, 0.095 at checkpoint 3000, and 0.114 at both checkpoints 4000 and 5000.
Recovery halts entirely between checkpoints 4000 and 5000, plateauing 15\% below the vanilla baseline of 0.134 with no further improvement.
ActAdd~\citep{turner2023actadd}, the inference-time baseline, achieves only $\sycon = 0.054$, confirming that activation-level intervention without weight updates cannot resolve the calibration problem.
$\rthree$-only GRPO exhibits the same stubbornness pattern as the $\dsyc$ approaches (high $\nof$, near-zero $\tof$) at milder severity.
The sparse scalar reward per completion cannot teach the model \emph{which} belief changes are warranted: it collapses an entire multi-turn exchange into one number that does not distinguish legitimate resistance from stubborn refusal.

\paragraph{Why SFT succeeds where GRPO fails.}
ACT~\citep{consistency2025bctact} achieves $\sycon = 0.301$ at checkpoint 8000, more than $2{\times}$ the vanilla baseline and above every RL and inference-time variant (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}).
The ACT trajectory is not monotonic: $\sycon = 0.255$ at checkpoint 2000, dips to 0.214 at checkpoint 4000 ($-4.1$ percentage points as $\tof$ drops and $\nof$ rises), recovers to 0.262 at checkpoint 6000, and reaches 0.301 at checkpoint 8000.
ACT also experiences stubbornness episodes, yet it recovers from them.
The critical difference is supervision density.
SFT provides a corrective gradient at every token position in every training example: when the model begins to resist valid corrections, per-token cross-entropy loss immediately penalizes the incorrect tokens and supplies gradient information about \emph{which} outputs need to change.
GRPO provides one scalar per completion; once the policy locks into stubbornness, that scalar reinforces the behavior because consistent non-flipping collects high reward from both $\rone$ and $\rthree$.
Dense per-token loss can break out of stubbornness equilibria that sparse per-completion reward cannot escape.
This recovery capacity is the practical signature of the dense-versus-sparse supervision gap.
ACT is also far more efficient: its checkpoint 500 ($\sycon = 0.170$) already exceeds the plateau that $\rthree$-only GRPO reaches after 5000 steps of training.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
These results point to several open problems.
First, condition-aware reward design could jointly encode belief-change direction and evidential warrant by conditioning on whether the input challenge provides valid grounds for revision.
Second, hybrid pipelines that apply SFT to establish the valid/invalid distinction as a warm start, followed by RL for broader distributional coverage, may combine the calibration quality of dense supervision with the exploration benefits of reinforcement learning.
Third, process reward models that provide per-step feedback within the RL framework could bridge the supervision density gap and retain online optimization.
Beyond sycophancy, the principle that discriminability does not guarantee reward utility applies to any behavioral attribute where the target and its complement share the same geometric direction~\citep{skalse2022hacking}.
Whether this principle extends to other alignment-relevant behaviors, such as hallucination and instruction-following, is an important open question.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

This work tested a natural hypothesis: that a representation direction capable of detecting sycophantic behavior should also serve as an effective reward signal for training against it. Our experiments systematically falsify this hypothesis across multiple formulations and reveal a structural barrier that applies beyond any single reward design.

We first established that \dsyc{} achieves strong offline discriminability (AUROC 0.82 on Qwen3-8B, 0.78 on Llama-3-8B) with cross-model transfer, confirming that contrastive directions do capture a real geometric signature of sycophantic capitulation. Yet all three reward formulations built on this direction failed across six GRPO configurations. The cosine reward could not separate valid revisions from sycophantic ones in the narrow online activation gap. The probe reward produced a stubbornness trap: the policy reached \tof{}$= 0$ by step 500, with entropy collapse following only 1{,}300 steps later, exposing a dangerous dissociation between behavioral failure and standard training monitors. Even removing \dsyc{} entirely and training with the behavioral \rthree{} reward alone yielded a \sycon{} plateau at 0.114, below the vanilla baseline of 0.134.

The root cause is consistent across all configurations: \dsyc{} encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}. Valid revision and sycophantic capitulation occupy overlapping geometric regions because they share the same surface behavior; they differ only in evidential warrant, which no single activation direction can encode. That Activation Consistency Training achieves \sycon{}$= 0.301$ through dense per-token supervision confirms that the missing ingredient is token-level teaching of \emph{which} belief changes are appropriate, not a better reward scalar.

The broader lesson extends beyond sycophancy: representation geometry that reliably detects a behavior is not automatically suitable for optimizing against it. Any alignment effort that converts a detection probe into a reward signal must verify that the probe separates not only the target behavior from its complement, but also the valid and invalid instances within each class. Without this finer distinction, RL will find the shortest path to reward, and that path leads away from the intended objective.
